overview.intro: The Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) was the first long-lasting Muslim state of northern India, ruled by five dynasties over three centuries. This chapter studies the sources - inscriptions and the Qutab Minar - the dynasties in chronological order, and the two rulers the syllabus singles out: Alauddin Khilji (market regulations, Deccan expedition, measures against the nobility, military and revenue reforms) and Muhammad Bin Tughlaq (transfer of capital, token currency, taxation in the Doab, plan of conquests).

blocks.text: Mahmud of Ghazni's raids (1000-1027) exposed India's wealth; Muhammad Ghori's victories (Tarain 1191-92) conquered the north-west. After Ghori's death in 1206, his slave-general Qutbuddin Aibak founded an independent Sultanate at Delhi. For 320 years five dynasties ruled - the Mamluk (Slave), Khilji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi - repelling Mongol invasions, building Indo-Islamic architecture, and centralising power over north India, until Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526.

Sources. Inscriptions: foundation and mosque inscriptions (e.g., the Ala-i-Darwaza records of Alauddin's era, Balban's inscriptions) document rulers, dates and buildings. The Qutab Minar is the standing monument-source: begun in 1199 by Qutbuddin Aibak and completed by Iltutmish (a fourth storey added later by Firuz Shah Tughlaq), it rises about 72.5 metres, its sandstone bands carrying Quranic verses and builders' records - the tallest brick minaret of its age and the emblem of Sultanate architecture. Chronicles such as Barani's Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi and Ibn Battuta's Rihla supply narrative detail, though the syllabus prescribes inscriptions and the Qutab Minar.

Dynasties in chronological order. Mamluk/Slave (1206-1290): Qutbuddin Aibak (founder; began Qutab Minar), Iltutmish (real consolidator: tanka-jital currency, iqta system, completed the Minar, faced Mongols), Raziya (first and only woman ruler, 1236-40), Balban (divine-right kingship, spy system, restored majesty). Khilji (1290-1320): Jalaluddin (mild), Alauddin (greatest Sultan of the line - see below). Tughlaq (1320-1414): Ghiyasuddin (canals, Tughlaqabad), Muhammad Bin Tughlaq (the experimenter), Firuz Shah (welfare works, canals, hospitals). Sayyid (1414-1451): Khizr Khan and successors holding Delhi after Timur's invasion. Lodi (1451-1526): Bahlul, Sikandar (founded Agra), Ibrahim (last Sultan, defeated at Panipat).

Alauddin Khilji - market regulations. To maintain a huge standing army paid in cash, Alauddin fixed the prices of grain, cloth, horses, cattle, slaves, meat and vegetables in the markets of Delhi, set up the diwan-i-riyasat and shahna-i-mandi to enforce them, built royal grain stores, and standardised weights and measures with severe punishment for cheating. Barani records that prices stayed stable even in drought years - the boldest medieval experiment in state-run market control.

Alauddin - measures against the nobility. Believing that rebellion is born of wealth and intrigue, Alauddin confiscated all religious endowments and grants of land, took back excess riches, banned wine-drinking and social gatherings among nobles, forbade inter-marriage between noble families without royal permission, and posted an extensive spy network over every officer. The nobility became wholly dependent on state service - rebellion within his reign was rare.

Alauddin - Deccan expedition. Between about 1307 and 1312, the Sultan's general Malik Kafur led armies into the Deccan and far south: Devagiri (Yadavas), Warangal (Kakatiyas), Dwarasamudra (Hoysalas) and Ma'bar (Pandyas) were defeated and forced to pay huge tribute, with immense booty of gold, jewels and elephants. Alauddin took the title Sikandar-i-Sani ('second Alexander') and became the first Muslim ruler to extend sway to the tip of the peninsula - through raid-and-tribute rather than annexation.

Alauddin - military and revenue reforms. Military: a permanent standing army paid directly from the treasury; regular reviews with chehra (descriptive roll of each soldier) and dagh (branding of horses) to prevent fake musters; a central registry of troops and a large cavalry with the arsenal under state care. Revenue: land was measured; the state's demand was fixed at half the produce, collected directly by amils from cultivators, removing powerful intermediaries; additional taxes were levied on cattle and houses. These reforms paid for the army and the price controls together.

Muhammad Bin Tughlaq - transfer of capital. To control the Deccan better, he ordered the capital moved from Delhi to Devagiri, renamed Daulatabad (c. 1327), and compelled the population to march with it; after a few years he ordered a return. The experiment failed - immense suffering, ruined Delhi's trade, and won the Sultan a reputation for caprice - though its strategic aim (a more central capital) had logic.

Muhammad Bin Tughlaq - token currency. Around 1330, short of silver, he issued copper tokens declared equal to the tanka, imitating an earlier Chinese practice. But the state could not prevent private minting: forgery flooded the market, foreign traders refused the tokens, and the Sultan had to withdraw them, exchanging good silver for the copper - a heavy financial loss.

Muhammad Bin Tughlaq - taxation in the Doab. To raise revenue, he increased taxation in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab - but the measure coincided with famine. Peasants ruined by the demands abandoned their fields, revolt spread, and the Sultan had to retreat: tax relief, loans and well-digging schemes came too late to restore confidence.

Muhammad Bin Tughlaq - plan of conquests. He raised an enormous army for the conquest of Khurasan (Persia) - which then became unnecessary as conditions changed - and launched the Qarachil (Kumaon-Himalayan) expedition, which suffered terrible losses. His conquest plans exhausted the treasury and brought him a reputation for wild ambition; his intelligence, learning and even administrative ability (Ibn Battuta describes the efficiency of his post system) could not save his reputation or, finally, his dynasty's grip.

items: Qutbuddin Aibak - Founder of the Sultanate (1206); began the Qutab Minar; died in a polo accident.
Iltutmish - Real consolidator: tanka-jital currency, iqta system, completed the Qutab Minar; saved Delhi from Mongols by diplomacy.
Raziya Sultan - First and only woman on Delhi's throne (1236-40); capable, but nobles' prejudice brought her down.
Balban - Restored royal prestige with divine-right kingship and a stern spy system.
Alauddin Khilji - Market controls, revenue and army reforms; Deccan and south conquests; Sikandar-i-Sani.
Muhammad Bin Tughlaq - The learned experimenter: Daulatabad transfer, token currency, Doab taxation, conquest plans.
Firuz Shah Tughlaq - Welfare works: canals, hospitals, charity department; added a storey to the Qutab Minar.
Ibn Battuta - Moroccan traveller (1333-42 in India) whose Rihla describes the court of M.B. Tughlaq.
Ghurid conquests left a Turkish military class needing a state of its own.
Mongol pressure from the north-west demanded a strong central army.
The iqta system and bandagan (loyal slave-officers) gave cheap, centralised control.
Urbanisation and the cash economy enabled market regulation and coinage reforms.
Indo-Islamic architecture (arch, dome, minaret) and new urban culture took root.
Persianate administration, coinage (tanka) and iqta revenue entered Indian practice.
Alauddin's controls proved the state could intervene in markets for military ends.
M.B. Tughlaq's failures weakened the centre, opening the way to provincial kingdoms.
The Sultanate fell at Panipat (1526), clearing the path for the Mughals.

blocks.text: Dagh vs Chehra: Branding of horses versus descriptive rolls of soldiers in army reviews.
Alauddin's market regulations vs M.B. Tughlaq's token currency: Successful price controls enforced by stores and officers versus a failed monetary experiment wrecked by forgery.
Iqta vs Later Mughal jagir: Sultanate revenue assignment for service versus the Mughal salary-equivalent assignment; both non-hereditary.
Qutab Minar vs Ala-i-Minar: The completed 72.5 m minaret of Aibak/Iltutmish versus Alauddin's unfinished rival beside it.

items: Calling Aibak the 'real founder' - he founded it; Iltutmish consolidated it.
Placing Raziya in the Khilji dynasty - she was Mamluk (Slave dynasty).
Swapping dagh (horses) and chehra (soldiers).
Saying the token currency failed because copper was worthless - it failed through over-issue and forgery.
Writing that Alauddin's Deccan campaigns annexed the south - they were tribute raids, not annexations.
Claiming the capital transfer was purely mad - it had a strategic aim but disastrous execution.

questions.prompt: Who founded the Delhi Sultanate in 1206?
questions.explanation: A former slave-general of Muhammad Ghori; Iltutmish consolidated the state.
questions.commonMistake: Calling Iltutmish the founder - he is the 'real founder' in the sense of consolidator.

questions.prompt: The correct chronological order of the Sultanate dynasties is:
The 'dagh' system of Alauddin Khilji referred to:
questions.explanation: Chehra was the descriptive roll of soldiers; dagh branded the horses to prevent substitution.

questions.prompt: Who was the first and only woman ruler of Delhi?
questions.explanation: She defied convention but fell to noble prejudice.
questions.commonMistake: Naming Nur Jahan (a Mughal empress, never ruler).

questions.prompt: Which battle ended the Delhi Sultanate, and in which year?
questions.answer: The First Battle of Panipat, 1526 - Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi.
questions.explanation: It opened Mughal rule in India.
questions.commonMistake: Naming the Second Battle of Panipat (1556).

questions.prompt: Mention any two market regulations of Alauddin Khilji.
questions.answer: Any two of: prices of essential goods (grain, cloth, horses, slaves, meat) were fixed by the state; market controllers (shahna-i-mandi, diwan-i-riyasat) enforced prices, weights and measures; royal grain stores supplied Delhi; harsh punishment for short weights or cheating; merchants had to register and sell at fixed rates.
questions.explanation: Any two, with the enforcement mechanism.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing market rules with revenue rules.

questions.answer: The assignment of a territory's land revenue to a noble or officer (muqti/iqtadar) in return for military or administrative service; the muqti collected revenue, maintained troops, and remitted the balance to the Sultan. Iqtas were transferable and non-hereditary, keeping nobles dependent on the crown.

questions.prompt: Why did the token currency of Muhammad Bin Tughlaq fail?
questions.answer: The copper tokens were declared equal to the silver tanka, but the government did not restrict minting to the royal mint: private forgeries flooded the market, foreign traders refused the tokens, and home payments defaulted. The Sultan withdrew the issue, exchanging silver for tokens at face value - a huge loss.
questions.explanation: Over-issue and forgery are the keys.
questions.commonMistake: Saying copper was intrinsically useless - the flaw was control, not metal.

questions.prompt: Why did Alauddin Khilji regulate markets? Explain the connection with his army.
questions.answer: Alauddin maintained a huge permanent standing army paid in cash from the treasury. To pay for it without raising taxes ruinously, he had to keep prices low: if grain, horses, cloth and cattle were cheap, soldiers' salaries went far. Hence the market regulations - fixed prices, royal grain stores, controllers and severe punishment - and the linked revenue reforms measuring land and taking half the produce to fill the granaries. Market control was thus a fiscal-military device, not merely charity towards consumers.
questions.explanation: Army cost -> price control -> revenue supply chain.

questions.prompt: Compare the reforms of Alauddin Khilji with the experiments of Muhammad Bin Tughlaq.
questions.answer: Alauddin's measures succeeded because they were realistic and enforced: market prices were fixed and backed by state stores and spies; land was measured with half-produce revenue; the army was reviewed with dagh and chehra; nobles were subdued by confiscation and surveillance. Muhammad Bin Tughlaq's experiments were intellectually bold but failed in execution: the capital transfer to Daulatabad caused suffering and had to be rescinded; token currency collapsed through forgery; Doab taxation during famine provoked revolt; the Khurasan and Qarachil plans drained men and money. Both rulers centralised and innovated, but Alauddin matched ambition to capacity, while M.B. Tughlaq outran it.
questions.commonMistake: Calling M.B. Tughlaq simply mad - the failure was execution, not only design.

questions.prompt: Describe the measures taken by Muhammad Bin Tughlaq and state why most of them failed.
questions.answer: Transfer of capital: to control the Deccan he moved the capital from Delhi to Devagiri (Daulatabad) c. 1327, compelling the population to shift; the move caused enormous hardship, emptied Delhi, and was later reversed - it failed because distance and logistics defeated the strategic aim. Token currency: short of silver, he issued copper tokens equal to the tanka (c. 1330); the state could not monopolise minting, forgery flooded the market, and the scheme was withdrawn with silver-for-token exchange - failing through lack of mint control. Taxation in the Doab: to raise revenue he increased taxes in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab just as famine struck; ruined peasants abandoned land and revolted, forcing him to grant relief and loans - failing through wrong timing. Plan of conquests: a huge army raised for Khurasan stood idle as conditions changed, and the Qarachil (Kumaon) expedition suffered catastrophic losses - failing through miscalculation. His intelligence, learning and efficient administration (Ibn Battuta praises his post system) could not redeem schemes that outran the state's capacity.
questions.explanation: Each measure + specific reason for failure.
questions.commonMistake: Listing measures without reasons for failure.

questions.prompt: Give reasons: the Qutab Minar is an important source of Sultanate history.
questions.answer: Begun by Qutbuddin Aibak (1199) and completed by Iltutmish, with a later storey by Firuz Shah, the 72.5-metre minaret carries inscribed bands recording builders, dates and Quranic verses - primary evidence for the rulers and their chronology. Architecturally it evidences Indo-Islamic building technique (arch and dome tradition, calligraphic ornament), and its survival marks Delhi's rise as the Sultanate's capital. A standing monument of the period's own making, it corroborates the chronicles.
